states.name: New York
states.framework: NYDFS BitLicense / Limited Purpose Trust Charter; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202 (Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers)
states.regulator: New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS)
states.detail: Most coins commonly called “stablecoins” count as Virtual Currency under New York’s rules, which means issuing one requires a BitLicense or a New York-chartered trust company (the trust route also lets a company handle money transmission and fiduciary duties without extra licenses, which a BitLicense alone doesn’t allow). Before issuing, a coin also needs DFS sign-off through self-certification, a spot on DFS’s approved “Greenlist,” or individual approval. Coins already on the Greenlist include Gemini Dollar, Ripple USD, and WisdomTree Dollar. In July 2026, DFS proposed a new regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 202 (“Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers”), that reaffirms and aligns New York’s payment-stablecoin regime with the federal GENIUS Act. Part 202 takes effect on the GENIUS Act’s own effective date; it ties reserve, redemption, and attestation duties to the GENIUS Act (segregated per-brand reserves, monthly reserve-composition reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and an annual attestation), gives issuers already approved by DFS 12 months to reach full compliance, and withdraws the department’s June 8, 2022 stablecoin guidance as of its effective date.
states.effective: In force now under the BitLicense / limited-purpose trust charter and DFS’s June 8, 2022 stablecoin guidance; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202 takes effect on the GENIUS Act’s effective date (expected January 18, 2027) (replacing the 2022 guidance), with a 12-month compliance transition for existing issuers.
states.sourceText: NY DFS Virtual Currency Businesses; proposed 23 NYCRR Part 202, Authorized Payment Stablecoin Issuers (July 2026)
keyPoints: Today: hold a BitLicense or New York trust charter, and follow DFS’s 2022 stablecoin guidance (full 1:1 reserves, redemption at par, monthly CPA attestation)
Get DFS sign-off on the specific coin (self-certification, the approved Greenlist, or individual approval)
When Part 202 takes effect: back and segregate reserves per coin, file monthly reserve reports checked by an outside accounting firm, and get a yearly sign-off
Publish clear rules for how customers can cash out their coins
Already licensed? You have 12 months to meet the new Part 202 rules once they take effect
states.summary: New York already requires state approval to issue a stablecoin, and it already sets reserve, redemption, and attestation rules through existing DFS guidance. It has proposed updated rules (Part 202) that will replace that guidance and match the new federal GENIUS Act once the Act takes effect; firms already licensed then get a year to comply.

states.name: California
states.framework: Digital Financial Assets Law (DFAL)
states.regulator: California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI)
states.detail: California's Digital Financial Assets Law entered into force on July 1, 2026. Any exchange, custodian, stablecoin issuer, or Bitcoin ATM operator serving California residents must now hold a DFPI license or have filed a complete application, or face civil enforcement of up to $100,000 per day. The law bars licensees from exchanging a stablecoin unless its issuer is licensed, has applied for a license, or is a qualified bank or trust company backing the coin with eligible securities. DFPI expects an initial $100,000 net worth, subject to change, and began accepting applications through NMLS on March 9, 2026.
states.effective: In force since Jul. 1, 2026; DFPI license or complete application now required; enforcement active
states.sourceText: AB 39, Financial Code Div. 1.25

states.name: Texas
states.framework: Money Services Modernization Act (Finance Code Ch. 152)
states.detail: Texas treats qualifying stablecoins as 'money,' which means issuing or transmitting them requires a money transmission license. To count, a stablecoin must be pegged to a currency like the dollar, fully backed by reserve assets, and redeemable for that currency on demand. Licensees must hold a minimum net worth that scales with their size, starting at $100,000. Texas also lets a licensee hold stablecoin itself as part of its required reserves, as long as it's the same stablecoin it owes to customers and is kept in proper custody.
states.effective: In force since Sept. 1, 2023
states.sourceText: Tex. Finance Code Ch. 152, enacted by S.B. 895 (2023)

states.name: Florida
states.framework: Money services business licensing (Fla. Stat. ch. 560) reaching virtual currency now; Florida Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 175) adds a stablecoin-issuer license from Oct. 1, 2026; SB 1568 pilot; HB 505 kiosks
states.detail: Florida regulates money services businesses under Chapter 560 of the Florida Statutes, administered by the Office of Financial Regulation (OFR). Virtual currency is treated as “monetary value,” so transmitting or exchanging it for others generally requires a Chapter 560 license, a view the OFR aligned with after Florida v. Espinoza. A 2022 amendment (CS/HB 273), effective January 1, 2023, added a statutory definition of “virtual currency” and eased the rules for direct two-party transactions, so a seller selling virtual currency straight to a buyer no longer needs a license, while third-party transmission remains licensable. On top of this, Florida enacted a package of stablecoin laws signed by Governor DeSantis on June 27, 2026. HB 175, the Florida Payment Stablecoin Act, requires a license from the OFR before issuing a payment stablecoin, with reserves backed one-to-one by cash or similarly safe assets and verified monthly by a CPA, aligning the state with the federal GENIUS Act; its licensing provisions take effect October 1, 2026. SB 1568 establishes a Stablecoin Pilot Program letting the Department of Financial Services accept approved payment stablecoins for certain government fees, effective on enactment. HB 505 requires virtual-currency kiosk operators to register with the OFR. Payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Chapter 560 money-services licensing (reaching virtual currency; two-party VC sales exempt since Jan. 1, 2023) in force now; stablecoin package signed June 27, 2026, HB 175 issuer licensing effective Oct. 1, 2026; SB 1568 pilot and HB 505 kiosks effective on enactment
states.sourceText: Fla. Stat. ch. 560 (Money Services Businesses; virtual currency as monetary value; CS/HB 273 2022, eff. Jan. 1 2023); HB 175 Florida Payment Stablecoin Act (eff. Oct. 1, 2026); SB 1568 Stablecoin Pilot; HB 505 kiosks; FL Office of Financial Regulation
keyPoints: Today: hold a Florida money-services (Chapter 560) license to transmit or exchange virtual currency for others, through the Office of Financial Regulation
Direct two-party sales of virtual currency (seller straight to buyer) have been exempt from licensing since January 1, 2023 (CS/HB 273)
From October 1, 2026: to *issue* a payment stablecoin, get the new OFR license under HB 175, back reserves 1:1 with cash or safe assets, verified monthly by a CPA (aligned with the GENIUS Act)
Virtual-currency kiosk operators must register with the OFR (HB 505)
Florida is piloting acceptance of approved stablecoins for certain state fees (SB 1568)
states.summary: Florida already requires a state license to transmit or exchange virtual currency for others, though since 2023 a direct two-party sale (seller straight to buyer) is exempt. From October 1, 2026, a new law adds a dedicated license to *issue* a payment stablecoin, backed one-to-one by reserves checked monthly. Florida is also piloting acceptance of approved stablecoins for some state fees.

states.name: Wyoming
states.framework: Money-transmitter exemption for virtual currency (W.S. 40-22-104); Special Purpose Depository Institution charter (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.); Wyoming Stable Token Act (W.S. 40-31-101 through 40-31-109; SF0127 / Enrolled Act No. 85, 2023), under which the state issues its own stablecoin
states.detail: Wyoming is the most distinctive state regime, and it works in three layers. First, private activity is exempt: the Wyoming Money Transmitters Act exempts virtual currency from licensing, so buying, selling, issuing, or taking custody of payment instruments in the form of virtual currency, or receiving virtual currency for transmission, does not require a money-transmitter license (W.S. 40-22-104). Wyoming defines these categories precisely: under W.S. 34-29-101, digital assets fall into three mutually exclusive classes, digital consumer assets, digital securities, and virtual currency, and a payment stablecoin (a medium of exchange that is not legal tender) generally sits in the “virtual currency” class the exemption covers. Second, a chartered-bank route exists: Wyoming created the Special Purpose Depository Institution (SPDI), a state bank charter designed to custody and handle digital assets (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.), used by digital-asset banks such as Kraken Bank and Custodia. Third, and uniquely in the United States, the state issues its own stablecoin. Under the Wyoming Stable Token Act (W.S. 40-31-101 et seq.), the Wyoming Stable Token Commission issues the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT, launched as WYST in August 2025 and later rebranded), a virtual currency redeemable for one US dollar held in trust by the state (W.S. 40-31-104, 40-31-106). Under the Act’s reserve requirements as amended and the Commission’s rules, the token is backed only by cash, US Treasuries maturing within a year, or short-term Treasury repurchase agreements; a trust account holds 100% of the token’s notional value, plus a separate liquidity fund targeting a further 2% buffer, with surplus earnings directed quarterly to a state school foundation program. FRNT reached mainnet on August 18, 2025 and opened to public purchase on January 7, 2026 across eight blockchains. Private payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Virtual currency exempt from money-transmitter licensing (W.S. 40-22-104); SPDI charter available (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.); state-issued FRNT on mainnet since Aug. 18, 2025 and open to public purchase since Jan. 7, 2026
states.sourceText: W.S. 34-29-101 (digital-asset definitions: consumer asset / security / virtual currency); W.S. 40-22-104 (Money Transmitters Act virtual-currency exemption); W.S. 13-12-101 et seq. (SPDI charter); Wyoming Stable Token Act, W.S. 40-31-101 through 40-31-109 (SF0127 / Enrolled Act No. 85, 2023); Wyoming Stable Token Commission
keyPoints: No money-transmitter license is required to buy, sell, custody, or transmit virtual currency (including stablecoins) in Wyoming (W.S. 40-22-104)
Digital-asset banks can instead charter as a Special Purpose Depository Institution (SPDI) (W.S. 13-12-101 et seq.), the route used by Kraken Bank and Custodia
Wyoming itself issues a stablecoin, the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT), redeemable at $1.00 and fully reserved in cash and short US Treasuries
FRNT has been open to public purchase since January 7, 2026, live across eight blockchains
Private payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act
states.summary: Wyoming is deliberately crypto-friendly and distinctive. It does not require a money-transmitter license to buy, sell, custody, or transmit virtual currency, including stablecoins. Instead it built bespoke structures: a special digital-asset bank charter (SPDI) and, uniquely, its own state-issued stablecoin, the Frontier Stable Token (FRNT).

states.name: Illinois
states.framework: Digital assets: Digital Assets and Consumer Protection Act (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/) and Digital Asset Kiosks Act (DAKA, 205 ILCS 732/), plus the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/, enacted by SB 3019 / Public Act 104-0468). Money transmission: Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412), which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective Jan. 1, 2026.
states.regulator: Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR)
states.detail: Illinois has built a comprehensive digital-asset framework through four instruments, most of which phase in over 2026–2027. Money transmission was overhauled first: SB 3412 enacted the Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act and expressly repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective January 1, 2026 (§ 900-30), moving Illinois to NMLS-based multistate licensing. Illinois did not adopt the model act’s optional virtual-currency provisions, so the money-transmission statute does not expressly reach virtual-currency or stablecoin transmission. Digital assets are instead addressed by two laws signed August 18, 2025. The Digital Assets and Consumer Protection Act (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/, Public Act 104-0428) requires any person engaged in “digital asset business activity”, exchanging, transferring, or storing digital assets for Illinois residents, or digital-asset administration, to register with the Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR). Its “digital asset” definition is drawn to capture stablecoins: assets not marketed for investment are generally excluded, except where the instrument is marketed to hold a nominal value “so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed.” DACPA’s prohibitions are not enforced until January 1, 2027, and registration is not required until July 1, 2027 (implementing rules may not take effect before January 1, 2026). The Digital Asset Kiosks Act (DAKA, 205 ILCS 732/, Public Act 104-0429) requires crypto-kiosk operators to register with IDFPR, caps daily kiosk transactions at $2,500 for new customers and $10,500 for existing customers, limits per-transaction fees to the greater of $5 or 18%, and mandates disclosures; existing operators must register by July 1, 2027. Finally, the Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/), enacted as Article 3 of the FY2027 revenue bill (SB 3019, Public Act 104-0468), imposes, beginning January 1, 2027, a 0.2% tax on the privilege of receiving digital-asset business activity (exchanging, transferring, or storing digital assets) by an Illinois customer, collected by “digital asset brokers” (defined by reference to IRC § 6045(c)(1)(D)) and reaching out-of-state brokers whose gross receipts from Illinois customers reach $100,000 or more, tested quarterly. Returns and payment are due monthly, on or before the 20th, and the tax is administered by the Illinois Department of Revenue (the Act adopts DACPA’s definition of “digital asset,” so its stablecoin coverage carries into the tax). Illinois is therefore classified as phasing in: the dedicated regime is enacted but its core registration, kiosk, and tax obligations are not enforced until 2027.
states.effective: DACPA/DAKA core obligations enforced Jan. 1, 2027 and registration required by Jul. 1, 2027 (agency rules no earlier than Jan. 1, 2026); DATA (0.2% tax) effective Jan. 1, 2027 with broker registration before then; MTMA (SB 3412) effective Jan. 1, 2026 (Transmitters of Money Act repealed).
states.sourceText: “‘Digital asset’ … does not include … (4) A digital representation of value that is not marketed, used, promoted, offered, or sold for investment or speculation, except that this exclusion shall not apply to any digital representation of value that … (B) is marketed … in a manner that intends to establish a reasonable expectation or belief among the general public that the instrument will retain a nominal value that is so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed.” (DACPA, 205 ILCS 731/)
keyPoints: Today: money transmission is governed by the new Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412), which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act effective Jan. 1, 2026; Illinois did not adopt the model act’s optional virtual-currency provisions, so the money-transmission law does not expressly license virtual-currency or stablecoin transmission

From Jan. 1, 2027, DACPA (205 ILCS 731/): businesses that exchange, transfer, store, or administer digital assets for Illinois residents must register with IDFPR; the “digital asset” definition expressly captures stablecoins (instruments marketed to hold a nominal value “so stable as to render the nominal value effectively fixed”). Prohibitions enforced Jan. 1, 2027; registration required by Jul. 1, 2027

DAKA (205 ILCS 732/): crypto-kiosk operators must register with IDFPR; daily caps of $2,500 (new customers) and $10,500 (existing); per-transaction fees capped at the greater of $5 or 18%; existing operators register by Jul. 1, 2027

Digital Asset Tax Act (DATA, 35 ILCS 195/; SB 3019 / Public Act 104-0468, Art. 3): a 0.2% tax on the privilege of receiving digital-asset business activity (exchange, transfer, storage/custody) by a customer in Illinois, collected by “digital asset brokers,” reaching remote brokers with at least $100,000 in annual Illinois receipts (tested quarterly); returns and payment due monthly by the 20th; effective Jan. 1, 2027 (administered by the Illinois Department of Revenue)
states.summary: Illinois has enacted a comprehensive digital-asset framework, a consumer-protection registration law (DACPA), a crypto-kiosk law (DAKA), and the nation's first state digital-asset transaction tax (DATA), but the core obligations are not yet enforced and phase in over 2026–2027. Today, Illinois money-transmission law (the new Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act, which repealed the Transmitters of Money Act on Jan. 1, 2026) does not expressly reach virtual-currency transmission. From 2027, digital-asset businesses, stablecoin activity included, must register with IDFPR, and the transaction tax takes effect.

states.name: Colorado
states.framework: Model Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 25-1201)
states.detail: Colorado repealed its old Money Transmitters Act and replaced it with the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act, enabling multistate licensing participation. Unlike Texas, Colorado writes no virtual currency or stablecoin language into the statute at all: 'monetary value' is defined simply as 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' leaving it to interpretation whether a given stablecoin activity falls within that generic definition. Its net worth formula is identical to Texas's, since both states adopted the same model law: $100,000 or 3% of assets up to $100 million, then a declining percentage above that.
states.effective: Signed Apr. 18, 2025; effective Aug. 6, 2025
states.sourceText: Colorado General Assembly, HB 25-1201

states.name: Washington
states.framework: Uniform Money Services Act
states.regulator: Washington State Department of Financial Institutions
states.detail: Washington's statute defines 'virtual currency' directly and writes it into the definition of 'money transmission' itself, so there's no separate crypto license, just the existing money transmitter framework. Virtual currency licensees face specific disclosure duties: fee schedules, whether funds are insured, a notice that virtual currency transfers are irrevocable, and how errors get resolved. The standard net worth formula (as low as $10,000) jumps to a $100,000 minimum specifically for companies that provide virtual currency storage, though that figure comes from the implementing regulation, not the statute itself.
states.effective: In force

states.name: Arizona
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 1580, 2022)
states.regulator: Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions
states.detail: Arizona replaced its old money transmitter statute with the CSBS model act in 2022 (SB 1580, Chapter 236). Like Colorado, the new statute defines 'monetary value' as simply 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' with no explicit virtual currency or stablecoin definition. Whether a given stablecoin activity triggers licensing depends on how Arizona DIFI interprets that generic definition. Cryptocurrency kiosk operators face separate, explicit requirements under A.R.S. 6-1236, including daily transaction caps of $2,000 for new customers and $10,500 for existing ones, mandatory fraud warnings, and blockchain analytics requirements. Net worth follows the same formula as Colorado and Texas: $100,000 or 3% of total assets up to $100 million.
states.effective: Signed May 20, 2022
states.sourceText: A.R.S. Title 6, Chapter 12 (SB 1580, Ch. 236, 2022)

states.name: Georgia
states.framework: Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272)
states.regulator: Georgia Department of Banking and Finance
states.detail: Georgia enacted the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272) in 2026, a dedicated licensing regime for payment stablecoin issuers, but it is not yet in force. Under Section 4, and subject to appropriations by the General Assembly, it becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027 or 120 days after the issuance of final federal GENIUS Act implementing regulations. The Act carves payment stablecoin issuance out of Georgia's existing money transmission laws and authorizes the Department of Banking and Finance to license issuers, on a framework the statute requires to be substantially similar to the GENIUS Act. Licensed issuers must back outstanding stablecoins one-to-one with liquid reserves held in trust for consumers and maintain redemption policies. Beginning July 18, 2028, it becomes unlawful to offer or sell a payment stablecoin in Georgia unless the issuer is a permitted, licensed, or federally qualified issuer. Separately, some virtual-currency money transmission already requires a license under O.C.G.A. Sec. 7-1-680 et seq.
states.effective: Enacted 2026; effective (subject to state appropriations) the earlier of Jan. 18, 2027 or 120 days after federal GENIUS Act final rules; issuer requirement from Jul. 18, 2028
states.sourceText: “Issuance of payment stablecoin shall not be considered to be money transmission as defined by Code Section 7-1-680.… Subject to appropriations by the General Assembly, this Act shall become effective upon the earlier of: (1) January 18, 2027; or (2) 120 days after the issuance of final implementing regulations for the GENIUS Act.” (HB 1272)
keyPoints: Today: transmitting or issuing a stablecoin requires a Georgia money transmitter license, “virtual currency” falls within the money-transmission definition (O.C.G.A. § 7-1-680), administered by the Department of Banking and Finance (recent enforcement: a Jan. 2026 cease-and-desist against a crypto-kiosk operator)

When the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act takes effect (the earlier of Jan. 18, 2027 or 120 days after final GENIUS Act rules, subject to state appropriations): only a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue a payment stablecoin, licensed by the Department on a framework the statute requires to be “substantially similar to the GENIUS Act”

Once effective: issuing a payment stablecoin is no longer “money transmission” under § 7-1-680, a permitted issuer needs no separate money-transmission license to issue, sell, or redeem (but still needs one for other money-transmission activity)
From July 18, 2028: it is unlawful to offer or sell a payment stablecoin in Georgia unless it is issued by a licensed, permitted, or state qualified payment stablecoin issuer
states.summary: Georgia has enacted a dedicated stablecoin-issuer licensing law, the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272), but it is not yet in force. Until it takes effect, issuing or transmitting a stablecoin in Georgia falls under the state's existing money-transmitter licensing. Once effective, stablecoin issuance moves to the new regime and is no longer treated as money transmission.

states.name: North Carolina
states.framework: Money Transmitters Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B)
states.regulator: North Carolina Office of the Commissioner of Banks
states.detail: North Carolina regulates stablecoin and virtual-currency activity through its Money Transmitters Act (Chapter 53, Article 16B), administered by the Office of the Commissioner of Banks (NCCOB). The statute expressly defines virtual currency and brings money transmission conducted in whole or in part in virtual currency, including maintaining control of virtual currency on behalf of others, within its licensing requirement. A person engaging in money transmission must obtain a license through NMLS; the license is perpetual but requires an annual NMLS renewal filing. North Carolina does not yet have a dedicated stablecoin-issuer statute. A separate bill, the Virtual Currency Kiosk Consumer Protection Act (HB 920), would place crypto-ATM operators under NCCOB supervision, with implementing rules due by December 1, 2026.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act in force; virtual currency covered; kiosk bill (HB 920) pending, rules due Dec. 1, 2026
states.sourceText: N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B (Money Transmitters Act); NC Office of the Commissioner of Banks

states.name: Connecticut
states.framework: Money Transmission Act (virtual currency revisions, PA 25-66 / HB 7082)
states.detail: Connecticut revised its money transmission law to regulate virtual currency, effective October 1, 2025, administered by the Department of Banking. A person engaged in virtual currency business in Connecticut, by receiving, transmitting, storing, or maintaining custody or control of virtual currency, must hold virtual currency of the same type and amount owed or obligated to each customer. Licensees may not lend, hypothecate, pledge, or otherwise use or encumber customer virtual currency without authorization, and the act extends risk-disclosure and receipt requirements to virtual currency transmitters and kiosk operators. Custody may be delegated only to parties qualified to hold it.
states.effective: In force since Oct. 1, 2025
states.sourceText: Conn. Public Act 25-66 (HB 7082); CT Dept. of Banking

states.name: Nevada
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21, 2023); virtual currency covered by FID guidance
states.detail: Nevada enacted the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act through A.B. 21 (2023), modernizing its money transmission law at NRS Chapter 671, but it did not adopt the model's optional virtual-currency title (Article XIII). NRS Chapter 671 therefore does not expressly mention virtual or digital currency. Instead, the Financial Institutions Division (FID), through published guidance, applies the money-transmission licensing requirement to entities that transmit or hold digital currency, by kiosk, mobile, internet, or other means. Under that guidance, Bitcoin ATM operators must hold a money transmitter license and bond, and licensees holding virtual currency are expected to keep enough of each type to cover outstanding customer obligations. Entities acting purely as digital-asset custodians may instead be regulated as trust companies under NRS Chapter 669. Nevada thus regulates digital assets case by case under its MTMA-based money transmission law rather than a bespoke virtual-currency framework.
states.effective: MTMA enacted via A.B. 21 (2023) at NRS Ch. 671; digital currency covered by FID guidance, not the optional Article XIII virtual-currency title
states.sourceText: NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21 (2023) adopting the CSBS Model MTMA without the optional virtual-currency title; digital currency covered by Nevada FID guidance

states.name: Maine
states.framework: Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112)
states.regulator: Maine Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection
states.detail: Maine enacted the Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112, signed April 2024), effective August 9, 2024, administered by the Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection. The Act addresses virtual currency: it defines virtual currency and brings 'virtual currency business activity', including exchanging, transferring, or storing virtual currency and virtual currency administration (issuing virtual currency redeemable for money or other value), within its licensing framework. A business engaged in virtual currency business activity in Maine is generally covered.
states.effective: Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112) in force since Aug. 9, 2024; virtual currency business activity covered
states.sourceText: Me. Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112); Maine Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection

states.name: New Hampshire
states.framework: Money Transmission Act (RSA 399-G)
states.detail: New Hampshire requires a money transmitter license under RSA 399-G, administered by the Banking Department, but RSA 399-G:3, VII expressly exempts persons who sell or issue payment instruments or stored value solely in the form of convertible virtual currency, or who receive convertible virtual currency for transmission. The Banking Department confirms it neither licenses nor supervises businesses dealing solely in convertible virtual currency, including a stablecoin. However, money transmitters that handle traditional fiat currency, or that transmit both fiat and cryptocurrency, still must be licensed. Even transactions solely involving cryptocurrency remain subject to New Hampshire's Consumer Protection Act (RSA 358-A), so exemption from licensing is not the same as being unregulated. New Hampshire adopted the virtual-currency exemption in 2017; federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: RSA 399-G:3, VII exempts persons dealing solely in convertible virtual currency from licensing (fiat-touching activity still licensed; RSA 358-A Consumer Protection Act still applies)
states.sourceText: N.H. RSA 399-G:3, VII; N.H. Banking Department position on crypto regulation and jurisdiction

states.name: Rhode Island
states.framework: Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 19-14)
states.regulator: Rhode Island Department of Business Regulation
states.detail: Rhode Island regulates money transmission under its Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Title 19, Chapter 19-14), administered by the Department of Business Regulation, and its currency-transmitter licensing applies to virtual currency. H.B. 7282 (2024) added Money Transmission Modernization Act provisions, including tangible-net-worth and permissible-investment requirements and consumer protections, for currency transmitters, including cryptocurrency. Businesses that transmit or hold virtual currency for others are generally covered.
states.effective: Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 19-14) in force; applies to virtual currency; MTMA provisions added by H.B. 7282 (2024)
states.sourceText: R.I. Gen. Laws Title 19, Ch. 19-14 (Currency Transmissions); H.B. 7282 (2024); R.I. Department of Business Regulation

states.name: New Jersey
states.framework: Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C); Digital Asset & Blockchain Technology Act (A3454, pending)
states.regulator: New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance
states.detail: New Jersey's treatment of virtual currency is unsettled. It licenses money transmission under the Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C), administered by the Department of Banking and Insurance, and historically regulated crypto firms as money transmitters, but virtual currency does not fit cleanly within the statutory definitions of 'money' or 'payment instrument,' making that application awkward. The Digital Asset and Blockchain Technology Act (A3454) is pending before the legislature (approved in committee, not enacted); if passed, it would move digital-asset licensing to the Bureau of Securities in the Division of Consumer Affairs, clarify that digital assets are not money-transmission instruments, and require a license for digital-asset business activity (custody, trading, transfer). Until then, whether pure virtual currency requires a New Jersey money transmitter license is not firmly settled. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C) in force but virtual-currency fit is awkward and unsettled; dedicated Digital Asset Business Act (A3454) pending, not enacted
states.sourceText: N.J.S.A. 17:15C; N.J. Dept. of Banking and Insurance; A3454 (pending); N.J. Bureau of Securities

states.name: Delaware
states.framework: Sale of Checks and Transmission of Money Act (5 Del. C. Ch. 23); Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act (SB 18, enacted 2026)
states.regulator: Delaware Office of the State Bank Commissioner
states.detail: Delaware currently requires a money transmitter license under its Sale of Checks and Transmission of Money Act (5 Del. C. Chapter 23, Sec. 2303), administered by the Office of the State Bank Commissioner, and applies it to virtual currency transmission in practice, with major digital-asset exchanges holding Delaware money transmitter licenses. In July 2026, Governor Meyer signed Senate Bill 18, the Delaware Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act, part of a banking-modernization package aligning Delaware with the federal GENIUS Act. SB 18 replaces Chapter 23 with a comprehensive licensing framework for money transmitters and virtual currency businesses, including stablecoins. It takes effect the earlier of one year after enactment (around July 2027) or when the State Bank Commissioner promulgates final regulations.
states.effective: Sale of Checks Act (Ch. 23) in force and applied to virtual currency; SB 18 signed July 2026, effective the earlier of 1 year after enactment (~July 2027) or upon final regulations
states.sourceText: 5 Del. C. Ch. 23; Del. SB 18 (Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act, enacted 2026); Office of the State Bank Commissioner

states.name: Maryland
states.framework: Maryland Money Transmission Act (digital-asset authority via SB 759)
states.regulator: Maryland Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation
states.detail: Maryland regulates money transmission under the Maryland Money Transmission Act, administered by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation (OFR). OFR guidance confirms that receiving cryptocurrency from a customer and transferring it constitutes regulated money transmission, so virtual-currency businesses are generally licensed. Senate Bill 759 established explicit statutory authority to regulate digital assets under the Money Transmission Act, effective June 1, 2026. Virtual currency kiosk operators are separately regulated: a final rule effective March 30, 2026 (under Ch. 117 / S.B. 305, 2025) requires kiosk operators and each kiosk to register through NMLS.
states.effective: Money Transmission Act in force (OFR: crypto transmission licensed); digital-asset authority via SB 759 (eff. June 1, 2026); VC kiosk registration rule eff. Mar. 30, 2026
states.sourceText: Maryland Money Transmission Act; SB 759 (2026); Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation

states.name: Virginia
states.framework: Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 1942, Ch. 19.1)
states.regulator: Virginia State Corporation Commission, Bureau of Financial Institutions
states.detail: Virginia's Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 1942, enacted in 2025 as Acts of Assembly Chapter 214) takes effect July 1, 2026, replacing Chapter 19 of Title 6.2 with a new Chapter 19.1 administered by the State Corporation Commission's Bureau of Financial Institutions. Under Sec. 6.2-1922, 'money' does not include virtual currency, and because money transmission is defined in terms of money, payment instruments, and stored value, a business engaged solely in transmitting virtual currency, including a stablecoin, generally falls outside the licensing requirement. In practice the exclusion is narrower for stablecoins: activity that also moves fiat currency, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, transmits 'money' and can still be captured. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: MTMA (HB 1942, Acts ch. 214) effective July 1, 2026; virtual currency expressly excluded from 'money' (Sec. 6.2-1922, Ch. 19.1)
states.sourceText: Va. Code Sec. 6.2-1922 (Ch. 19.1, eff. Jul. 1, 2026; HB 1942 / Acts ch. 214); SCC Bureau of Financial Institutions

states.name: South Carolina
states.framework: South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Ch. 11; adopts the CSBS MTMA); S163 (2026) digital-asset exemptions
states.regulator: South Carolina Office of the Attorney General
states.detail: South Carolina regulates money transmission under the South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Chapter 11), administered through the Attorney General's Money Services Division. (The chapter, originally the Anti-Money Laundering Act, was renamed by 2024 Act No. 218, effective July 2, 2024, which substantially adopted the CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act without its optional virtual-currency title.) The statute does not expressly address virtual currency, and the Money Services Division's interpretive position is that virtual currency does not, by itself, qualify as 'monetary value,' so virtual currency alone is not money transmission. South Carolina reinforced this by statute in 2026 with S163, which provides that a person exchanging a digital asset for another digital asset without the exchange of legal tender or bank deposits, or engaged in digital-asset mining, node operation, or blockchain software development, is not required to obtain a money transmitter license (S163 also bars state use of a central bank digital currency and protects self-custody). The exclusion remains narrower for stablecoins in practice: activity involving legal tender, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, falls outside these exemptions and may require a license. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: Uniform Money Services Act in force (Division: VC not 'monetary value'); S163 (2026) statutorily exempts crypto-to-crypto without legal tender, mining, nodes, and blockchain development from money-transmitter licensing
states.sourceText: S.C. Code Title 35, Ch. 11 (Uniform Money Services Act); S.C. S163 (2026); Money Services Division

states.name: Massachusetts
states.framework: Money Transmission Law (Ch. 312 of the Acts of 2024; MGL c. 169B)
states.detail: Massachusetts overhauled its money transmission regime with Chapter 312 of the Acts of 2024, codified as MGL c. 169B ('Regulation of Money Transmission') and administered by the Division of Banks. The Division began licensing and regulating money transmitters under c. 169B effective January 1, 2026 (NMLS applications opened around July 1, 2025). The Division has stated that most common transactional virtual currencies, expressly including stablecoins such as USDC, are a form of 'monetary value' under c. 169B, Sec. 1, so virtual-currency transmission requires a license. Non-convertible or closed-loop currencies (for example, in-game currency) are not 'monetary value.' The law is consumer-protection focused, covering money transmission for personal, family, or household purposes.
states.effective: MGL c. 169B (Ch. 312, Acts of 2024); licensing effective Jan. 1, 2026; Division treats transactional virtual currency including USDC as 'monetary value' (licensed)
states.sourceText: Mass. Ch. 312, Acts of 2024 (MGL c. 169B, Sec. 1); Massachusetts Division of Banks FAQs

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.framework: Money Transmission Business Licensing Law, as amended by Act 7 of 2025
states.regulator: Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities
states.detail: Pennsylvania regulates money transmission under the Money Transmission Business Licensing Law, administered by the Department of Banking and Securities (DoBS), and virtual currency is now covered by statute. After 2019 DoBS guidance that virtual currency was not 'money' and a 2024 policy statement reversing that view, the legislature enacted Act 7 of 2025, which amended the law to expressly require a license to 'engage in the business of transmitting virtual currency ... for a fee' and retitled it to reference virtual currency. Entities that transmit virtual currency, including stablecoins, for a fee generally must be licensed, subject to exemptions such as transmission solely for personal or household use and certain self-hosted wallet activity. The Act takes effect 60 days after enactment (August 26, 2025), and DoBS rescinded its prior virtual-currency statement of policy. Note that a federally-permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI) is preempted by the GENIUS Act from Pennsylvania's licensing requirement for its stablecoin activity; non-issuer transmitters remain subject to it.
states.effective: Money Transmission Business Licensing Law as amended by Act 7 of 2025; effective 60 days after enactment (Aug. 26, 2025); virtual-currency transmission for a fee licensed by statute
states.sourceText: Pa. Act 7 of 2025 (Money Transmission Business Licensing Law); Pa. Dept. of Banking and Securities

states.name: District of Columbia
states.framework: Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Title 26, Ch. 10, Sec. 26-1001)
states.regulator: DC Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking (DISB)
states.detail: The District of Columbia requires a money transmitter license under its Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Title 26, Chapter 10; Sec. 26-1001), administered by the Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking (DISB). By DISB bulletin, and relying on United States v. Harmon (in which the court treated Bitcoin as functioning like money under the District's money-transmission definition), DISB considers Bitcoin and other virtual currency used as a medium of exchange, method of payment, or store of value to be money, so receiving for transmission, storing, or taking custody of virtual currency requires a license. Operating a virtual-currency kiosk or transmitting virtual currency without a license violates Sec. 26-1002 and can carry civil and criminal penalties.
states.effective: Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Sec. 26-1001 et seq.) in force; DISB treats virtual currency as money (per bulletin and U.S. v. Harmon); VC transmission/custody licensed
states.sourceText: D.C. Code Title 26, Ch. 10 (Sec. 26-1001 et seq.); DISB cryptocurrency & money transmission bulletin

states.name: Ohio
states.framework: Ohio Money Transmitters Act + DFI Interpretive Guidance 2022-01
states.detail: Ohio's Division of Financial Institutions treats businesses that buy, sell, or transmit cryptocurrency as money transmitters that must be licensed before serving Ohio customers. Interpretive Guidance 2022-01 covers crypto exchanges, kiosks/BTMs, and businesses with independent control over a customer's virtual currency. Stablecoin activity involving transmission or fiat conversion would require licensure on the same basis.
states.effective: Interpretive Guidance 2022-01, effective Aug. 31, 2022
states.sourceText: Ohio Div. of Financial Institutions, Money Transmitters

states.name: Michigan
states.framework: Michigan Money Transmission Services Act (Act 250 of 2006)
states.regulator: Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services (DIFS)
states.detail: Michigan's money-transmission law predates crypto and was never updated for it. DIFS's position is that cryptocurrency is not 'money' (not backed by tangible assets or insured deposits), so the pure-crypto leg falls outside DIFS authority. Fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-fiat transactions do require a money transmitter license, and major exchanges hold Michigan MT licenses. Treatment of stablecoins specifically remains unsettled.
states.effective: Act 250 of 2006 (no crypto-specific amendment)
states.sourceText: Michigan DIFS, Money Transmission Services

states.name: Tennessee
states.framework: Tennessee Money Transmitter Act + TDFI Virtual Currency Guidance
states.detail: TDFI's guidance is that cryptocurrency itself is not 'money,' so holding or transmitting pure virtual currency is not money transmission and the MT license does not cover VC transmission. However, converting crypto to or from sovereign currency through a third-party exchanger or automated machine IS money transmission requiring a license, and TDFI has stated that trade in stablecoins must be licensed as money transmission.
states.effective: TDFI Virtual Currency Guidance
states.sourceText: TN Dept. of Financial Institutions, Virtual Currency Guidance

states.name: Minnesota
states.framework: Minnesota Money Transmission Act (broad 'payment instrument' definition)
states.detail: Minnesota's money-transmission statute does not define 'money' and uses a broad 'payment instrument' definition understood to reach virtual currency, so a money transmitter license is required for VC transmission, and major exchanges hold Minnesota licenses. Treatment applies under the general statute rather than a crypto-specific law.
states.effective: Under existing Money Transmission Act (no separate VC statute confirmed)
states.sourceText: Minnesota Dept. of Commerce, Money Services Business
states.mtma: One of only two states to adopt the MTMA’s optional virtual-currency provisions (Title XIII), which expressly bring virtual-currency business under money-transmitter licensing (eff. Aug. 1, 2023)

states.name: Missouri
states.framework: Missouri Sale of Checks Law / money transmission (no VC-specific guidance)
states.detail: Missouri's Division of Finance has not published virtual-currency-specific guidance. A money transmitter (Sale of Checks) license is likely required where fiat currency is involved, and at least one major exchange holds a Missouri Sale of Checks license, but the treatment of pure crypto and stablecoins is unsettled absent specific guidance.
states.effective: No VC-specific guidance issued
states.sourceText: Missouri Division of Finance

states.name: Oregon
states.framework: Oregon Money Transmission Law (ORS 717.205)
states.detail: Oregon requires a money transmission license to conduct a money transmission business (ORS 717.205), and the Division of Financial Regulation applies this to cryptocurrency businesses transmitting value for Oregon customers. Stablecoin transmission and fiat conversion would require licensure on the same basis.
states.effective: Under ORS 717 (money transmission license required)
states.sourceText: Oregon Div. of Financial Regulation, Money Transmitter Licensing

states.name: Indiana
states.framework: Indiana Money Transmission (DFI: VC exchange exempt)
states.detail: The Indiana Department of Financial Institutions has stated that a money transmitter license is not required for a fiat or virtual currency exchange where the consumer is strictly buying or selling currency and cannot send fiat to another consumer. A virtual currency exchange therefore does not generally require an Indiana money transmitter license.
states.effective: Per DFI money transmitter licensing FAQ (NMLS)
states.sourceText: Indiana Dept. of Financial Institutions (money transmitter FAQ)

states.name: Iowa
states.framework: Iowa money transmission + Division of Banking VC guidance
states.detail: Iowa's Division has held that virtual currency qualifies as 'monetary value,' so receiving virtual currency for transmission in Iowa requires a money transmission license, and the Division has issued guidance for virtual currency kiosks. Major exchanges (Coinbase, Binance, Gemini) are registered as money transmitters in Iowa.
states.effective: Per Division of Banking guidance (VC = monetary value)
states.sourceText: Iowa Division of Banking, Guidance for Virtual Currency Kiosks

states.name: Kansas
states.framework: Kansas Money Transmitter Act + OSBC Guidance (MT 2014-01)
states.regulator: Kansas Office of the State Bank Commissioner
states.detail: Kansas OSBC guidance states that an entity engaged solely in the transmission of cryptocurrency is not required to obtain a license, and that exchanging one cryptocurrency for another, or transferring cryptocurrency between accounts, does not by itself qualify as money transmission because crypto is not 'money.' Transactions involving sovereign currency (fiat) can still trigger licensing.
states.effective: OSBC Cryptocurrency Guidance MT 2014-01
states.sourceText: Kansas Office of the State Bank Commissioner, Guidance MT 2014-01

states.name: Kentucky
states.framework: Kentucky money transmission (transmission of money or monetary value)
states.detail: Kentucky requires a license to operate a money transmission business, covering the transmission of money or monetary value by any means, which is understood to reach cryptocurrency businesses transmitting value for Kentucky customers. Treatment applies under the general money transmission statute rather than a crypto-specific law.
states.effective: Under Kentucky money transmission statute
states.sourceText: Kentucky Dept. of Financial Institutions, Money Transmission

states.name: Hawaii
states.framework: Hawaii Money Transmitters Modernization Act (Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 489D); digital-currency activity no longer requires a state money-transmitter license (effective July 1, 2024)
states.detail: Hawaii does not require a state money-transmitter license for digital-currency activity. After running the Digital Currency Innovation Lab (DCIL) as a pilot, the Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, Division of Financial Institutions concluded the DCIL on June 30, 2024 and determined that, effective July 1, 2024, its Money Transmitters Modernization Act no longer applies to cryptocurrency activity, so digital-currency companies may operate in Hawaii without a state money-transmitter license. Federal registration and licensing still apply, and a company that also transmits U.S. dollars still needs a money-transmitter license for that fiat activity. Payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: DCIL concluded June 30, 2024; no state money-transmitter license required for digital-currency activity as of July 1, 2024
states.sourceText: Hawaii DCCA/DFI release concluding the Digital Currency Innovation Lab (effective July 1, 2024); Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 489D

states.name: Alabama
states.framework: Alabama Monetary Transmission Act (Ala. Code § 8-7A-2, § 8-7A-5). The definition of “monetary value” in § 8-7A-2 expressly includes virtual currency.
states.detail: Alabama requires a license to sell or issue payment instruments or stored value, or to receive money or monetary value for transmission (Ala. Code § 8-7A-5). The Alabama Monetary Transmission Act defines “monetary value” as “a medium of exchange, including virtual or fiat currencies, whether or not redeemable in money” (Ala. Code § 8-7A-2), so transmitting or exchanging virtual currency for others requires a money-transmitter license. The Act is administered by the Alabama Securities Commission.
states.effective: Money-transmitter license required; “monetary value” expressly covers virtual currency
states.sourceText: “MONETARY VALUE. A medium of exchange, including virtual or fiat currencies, whether or not redeemable in money.” (Ala. Code § 8-7A-2)

states.name: Alaska
states.framework: Alaska Uniform Money Services Act (AS 06.55; definitions at AS 06.55.990, license required at AS 06.55.101). Virtual-currency business activity requires a money-transmitter license; the earlier Limited Licensing Agreement approach was discontinued as of January 2023.
states.regulator: Alaska Division of Banking and Securities
states.detail: Alaska requires virtual-currency business activity to be licensed as money transmission under the Alaska Uniform Money Services Act (AS 06.55). “Money services” and “monetary value” are defined in AS 06.55.990, and a license is required under AS 06.55.101. Previously the Division of Banking and Securities handled virtual-currency firms through a separate Limited Licensing Agreement, but that approach ended in January 2023: virtual-currency business activity now requires full money-transmitter licensure under AS 06.55 unless exempt. The Division of Banking and Securities administers the Act.
states.effective: Money-transmitter license plus Limited Licensing Agreement required for virtual-currency business
states.sourceText: Alaska Uniform Money Services Act, AS 06.55 (definitions, AS 06.55.990; license required, AS 06.55.101).

states.name: Arkansas
states.framework: Arkansas Uniform Money Services Act (A.C.A. § 23-55-102). “Money transmission” expressly includes receiving virtual currency for transmission; Act 557 of 2025 added virtual-currency kiosk provisions.
states.detail: Arkansas’s Uniform Money Services Act defines “money transmission” to include “receiving money, virtual currency, or monetary value for transmission” (A.C.A. § 23-55-102), so transmitting virtual currency for others generally requires a money-transmitter license from the Arkansas Securities Department, which administers the Act. Act 557 of 2025 amended the statute to add definitions and consumer-protection requirements for virtual-currency kiosks. The Department has at times issued no-action letters relieving specific digital-asset businesses of licensure.
states.effective: Money transmission expressly includes virtual currency; licensing required subject to case-by-case no-action letters
states.sourceText: “‘Money transmission’ means selling or issuing payment instruments, stored value, or prepaid access, or receiving money, virtual currency, or monetary value for transmission…” (A.C.A. § 23-55-102)

states.name: Idaho
states.framework: Idaho Money Transmitters Act (Idaho Code § 26-2902 (definitions), § 26-2903 (license required)). The Department of Finance treats virtual-currency exchange for fiat as licensable money transmission.
states.detail: Idaho requires a money-transmitter license to engage in the business of money transmission (Idaho Code § 26-2903), subject to the exemptions in § 26-2904. The Department of Finance takes the position that a virtual-currency exchanger who accepts fiat currency for later delivery in connection with a virtual-currency purchase must be licensed as a money transmitter, so virtual-currency exchange is generally licensable. The Department has at times issued no-action letters relieving particular businesses, such as certain digital-currency ATMs, from licensing, so treatment can be activity-specific. The Department of Finance administers the Act.
states.effective: Department of Finance requires money-transmitter licensing for virtual-currency exchange; activity-specific no-action letters issued
states.sourceText: Idaho Money Transmitters Act: a license is required to engage in money transmission (Idaho Code § 26-2903); the Department of Finance treats virtual-currency exchange for fiat as licensable money transmission.

states.name: Louisiana
states.framework: Louisiana Virtual Currency Businesses Act (La. Rev. Stat. §§ 6:1381–6:1394); dedicated standalone virtual-currency license via the Office of Financial Institutions
states.detail: Louisiana runs one of the most developed state regimes: the Virtual Currency Businesses Act (VCBA), La. Rev. Stat. §§ 6:1381 to 6:1394, adopted in 2020, made Louisiana the second state after New York to create a dedicated, standalone licensing scheme for virtual-currency business activity. A license (or equivalent permission) from the Office of Financial Institutions (OFI), applied for through NMLS, is required to conduct virtual-currency business activity with Louisiana residents. Licensing thresholds were tightened in 2023: SB 185 / Act 331 rescinded the former de minimis exception (§ 6:1389), so a license is required regardless of transaction volume. The Act lists exceptions in § 6:1383(B) and (C) (for example, virtual currency regulated under Louisiana securities law and personal or academic use). Requirements include a business plan, FinCEN registration and BSA/AML compliance, control-person background checks, a surety bond, and minimum net worth of the greater of $100,000 or 3% of total assets. The VCBA sits alongside the traditional money-transmitter license, and OFI’s 2014 guidance already treated virtual-currency exchangers as requiring money-transmitter licensing.
states.effective: VCBA licensing in force (license required to operate after June 30, 2023); de minimis exception removed by SB 185 / Act 331 (2023)
states.sourceText: La. Rev. Stat. §§ 6:1381–6:1394 (Virtual Currency Businesses Act); SB 185 / Act 331 (2023); LA Office of Financial Institutions.

states.name: Montana
states.framework: No Montana money-transmitter licensing statute: Montana does not license money transmitters. Affirmative digital-asset laws include SB 178 (2023) and SB 265 (2025).
states.regulator: None, no money transmitter licensing statute
states.detail: Montana is the only state with no money-transmitter licensing regime: the Division of Banking and Financial Institutions does not license money transmitters, so there is no state money-transmitter license requirement for transmitting or exchanging fiat or virtual currency, including stablecoins. Montana has instead legislated affirmatively on digital assets: SB 178 (2023) addresses the treatment of digital assets and protects crypto mining, and SB 265 (2025), the Financial Freedom and Innovation Act, protects the right to use digital assets and self-hosted wallets and bars state use of a central bank digital currency. Firms operating from Montana remain subject to federal money-services-business registration with FinCEN under the Bank Secrecy Act.
states.effective: No state money-transmission licensing; federal FinCEN/BSA still applies
states.sourceText: Montana has no money-transmitter licensing statute (Division of Banking and Financial Institutions); digital-asset laws include SB 178 (2023) and SB 265 (2025), the Financial Freedom and Innovation Act.

states.name: South Dakota
states.framework: South Dakota money transmission law (SDCL 51A-17-1(13)); Division of Banking treats “monetary value” as including virtual currency
states.detail: South Dakota treats “monetary value” under SDCL 51A-17-1(13) as including virtual currency, per the Division of Banking’s 2019 guidance on virtual-currency transmission, so persons in the business of transmitting virtual currency must obtain a money-transmitter license. Payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Money-transmitter license required; Division of Banking guidance (2019) treats “monetary value” as covering virtual currency
states.sourceText: SDCL 51A-17-1(13); SD Division of Banking, “Virtual Currency Transmission in South Dakota” (2019).

states.name: North Dakota
states.framework: North Dakota Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 2119, 2023; N.D.C.C. ch. 13-09.1), including the model act’s virtual-currency provisions
states.regulator: North Dakota Department of Financial Institutions
states.detail: North Dakota enacted the Money Transmission Modernization Act via SB 2119, signed March 15, 2023 and effective August 1, 2023, and is one of only two states (with Minnesota) to enact the model act’s virtual-currency title. The Act requires any person engaging in “virtual currency business activity” to obtain a money-transmitter license from the Department of Financial Institutions. Payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: MTMA with virtual-currency provisions effective August 1, 2023 (SB 2119)
states.sourceText: N.D.C.C. ch. 13-09.1 (Money Transmission Modernization Act, SB 2119, 2023); ND Department of Financial Institutions
states.mtma: One of only two states to adopt the MTMA’s optional virtual-currency provisions (Title XIII), which expressly bring virtual-currency business under money-transmitter licensing (SB 2119, eff. Aug. 1, 2023)

states.name: Nebraska
states.framework: Nebraska money transmission law (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 8-2715) covers virtual currency; Nebraska Financial Innovation Act creates state-chartered digital-asset depository institutions (§ 8-2724 exemption)
states.regulator: Nebraska Department of Banking and Finance
states.detail: Nebraska treats virtual currency as within money transmission: “monetary value” is defined as a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 8-2715), which encompasses digital currency, so money transmission involving virtual currency is licensable. Separately, the Nebraska Financial Innovation Act authorizes state-chartered “digital asset depository institutions,” which (effective Oct. 1, 2022) have the same exemption from money-transmission registration as other banks (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 8-2724) and can provide digital-asset custody and services under a dedicated charter with strong reserve and capital requirements. Payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Money transmission covers virtual currency; digital-asset depository charter effective Oct. 1, 2022 (Nebraska Financial Innovation Act)
states.sourceText: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 8-2715, § 8-2724 (Nebraska Financial Innovation Act); NE Dept. of Banking and Finance.

states.name: Oklahoma
states.framework: Oklahoma Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515) through Oct. 31, 2026; Oklahoma Money Transmission Modernization Act (6 O.S. § 1551) from Nov. 1, 2026, defining “money” to include qualifying stablecoins; digital-asset kiosks under § 1520.1
states.detail: Oklahoma licenses money transmission, and virtual-currency exchanges operating in the state hold Oklahoma money-transmitter licenses. Through October 31, 2026, licensing runs under the Oklahoma Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515), whose definition of “money transmitter” is fiat-centric: it reaches a person who accepts and transmits “currency or funds denominated in currency” (legal tender), or the value of that currency (6 O.S. § 1512). The Act does not expressly name virtual currency, so crypto firms are captured mainly through their fiat on- and off-ramp activity. The one express digital-asset provision is 6 O.S. § 1520.1 (SB 1083, 2025), regulating digital-asset kiosks (crypto ATMs): operators must be licensed as money transmitters, cap new-customer activity at $2,000 per day, limit aggregate fees to 15% per transaction, give prominent fraud warnings, provide receipts, refund fraudulently-induced customers, run blockchain-analytics screening, and employ a full-time compliance officer, with unlicensed operation a misdemeanor and kiosks subject to seizure by the Attorney General. Effective November 1, 2026, the Oklahoma Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 3521) repeals §§ 1511–1515 and recodifies money transmission at 6 O.S. § 1551, and, unlike the old act, expressly defines “money” to include a stablecoin that is (a) pegged to a sovereign currency, (b) fully backed by assets held in reserve, and (c) redeemable for sovereign currency from the issuer; the kiosk provisions (§§ 1520, 1520.1) are retained with their cross-reference updated. Non-stablecoin virtual currency (e.g., Bitcoin) is not “money” under either act. Payment-stablecoin issuance also remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515, fiat-centric) in force through Oct. 31, 2026; digital-asset kiosks expressly regulated under § 1520.1 (SB 1083, 2025); Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 3521) effective Nov. 1, 2026, recodifies at § 1551 and expressly adds qualifying stablecoins to “money”
states.sourceText: 6 O.S. § 1512 (Financial Transaction Reporting Act definitions, fiat-centric) and § 1520.1 (kiosks, SB 1083 2025); HB 3521 (enrolled) Oklahoma Money Transmission Modernization Act, § 55 repealer (§§ 1511–1515), § 56 eff. Nov. 1 2026, “money” incl. stablecoin (§ 1551)
keyPoints: Today (through Oct. 31, 2026): the Financial Transaction Reporting Act (6 O.S. §§ 1511–1515) licenses money transmission of currency/funds (fiat); it does not expressly name virtual currency, and crypto exchanges are licensed mainly for their fiat on/off-ramps

Crypto ATM / kiosk operators are expressly regulated (6 O.S. § 1520.1): licensed as money transmitters, $2,000/day new-customer cap, 15% fee cap, fraud warnings, receipts, and refunds, rules that continue after Nov. 1, 2026

From November 1, 2026: the Money Transmission Modernization Act (6 O.S. § 1551) replaces §§ 1511–1515 and, unlike the old law, defines “money” to include a stablecoin that is pegged to a sovereign currency, fully reserve-backed, and redeemable from the issuer
Non-stablecoin virtual currency (e.g., Bitcoin) is not “money” under either act, so its transmission is not squarely captured outside the kiosk rules
Separate federal track: issuing a payment stablecoin is governed by the GENIUS Act
states.summary: Oklahoma licenses money transmission, and crypto exchanges operating here hold Oklahoma licenses. The current law is fiat-focused and does not expressly name virtual currency; a modernized law effective November 1, 2026 writes fully-reserved, fiat-backed stablecoins directly into the legal definition of “money,” and crypto ATMs are separately regulated.

states.name: Utah
states.framework: Utah Money Transmitter Act (Utah Code § 7-25-102): the definition of “money transmission” excludes a blockchain token, so standalone virtual-currency transmission is not licensed. HB 72 (2026) carves virtual-currency kiosks back into licensing.
states.detail: Utah does not require a money-transmitter license for standalone virtual-currency transmission. The Money Transmitter Act’s definition of “money transmission” expressly excludes a “blockchain token” (Utah Code § 7-25-102), a 2020 change confirming that ordinary cryptocurrency transactions are not money transmission, so crypto firms are generally exempt. HB 72 (2026) creates an exception: operating a virtual-currency kiosk in Utah requires a license under the Money Transmitter Act and constitutes money transmission regardless of whether the transactions involve blockchain tokens. The Department of Financial Institutions administers the Act through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS).
states.effective: Express virtual-currency exclusion in the Money Transmitter Act; VC-kiosk operators licensed under HB 72 (2026), effective May 6, 2026
states.sourceText: Utah Code § 7-25-102 (definition of “money transmission” excludes a blockchain token); HB 72 (2026) requires virtual-currency kiosk operators to be licensed under the Money Transmitter Act.

states.name: New Mexico
states.framework: New Mexico Uniform Money Services Act (NMSA 1978 § 58-32-102 (definitions); § 58-32-201 (license required)). Virtual currency is reached by regulator interpretation of “monetary value,” not by an express virtual-currency statute.
states.regulator: New Mexico Financial Institutions Division (Regulation and Licensing Department)
states.detail: New Mexico requires a money-transmitter license to deal in virtual currency, reaching that result by regulator interpretation rather than express statute. The Uniform Money Services Act defines “money transmission” as receiving money or monetary value for transmission, and “monetary value” as “a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money” (NMSA 1978 § 58-32-102). The Regulation and Licensing Department’s Financial Institutions Division (FID) has stated that any business exchanging virtual currency for money, monetary value, or stored value for New Mexico residents must be licensed as a money transmitter under § 58-32-201.
states.effective: Uniform Money Services Act in force; FID interprets it to require money-transmitter licensing for virtual-currency exchange/transmission
states.sourceText: “Monetary value” means a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money (NMSA 1978 § 58-32-102); license required under § 58-32-201.

states.name: Mississippi
states.framework: Mississippi money transmission law (Miss. Code § 75-15-3; broad “monetary value” definition) and the Mississippi Money Transmission Modernization Act. Virtual-currency kiosk operators are licensed as money transmitters under HB 1625 (2026), effective July 1, 2026.
states.regulator: Mississippi Department of Banking and Consumer Finance
states.detail: Mississippi treats virtual-currency transmission as licensable money transmission. The statute defines “monetary value” as “a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money” (Miss. Code § 75-15-3), language broad enough to reach virtual currency, and major exchanges hold Mississippi money-transmitter licenses. HB 1625 (2026), the Mississippi Virtual Currency Kiosk Consumer Protection Act, makes this explicit for kiosks: a virtual-currency kiosk operator may not operate without a license under the Money Transmission Modernization Act and must comply with money-transmitter requirements, effective July 1, 2026, with the Department of Banking and Consumer Finance exercising authority over kiosk operators.
states.effective: Money transmission covers virtual currency via the broad “monetary value” definition; VC-kiosk operators licensed under HB 1625, effective July 1, 2026
states.sourceText: HB 1625 (2026), Mississippi Virtual Currency Kiosk Consumer Protection Act: virtual-currency kiosk operators must be licensed under the Money Transmission Modernization Act, effective July 1, 2026; “monetary value” defined at Miss. Code § 75-15-3.

states.name: West Virginia
states.framework: West Virginia Money Transmission Modernization Act (W. Va. Code § 32A-2-1 et seq., as amended by HB 5353 (2026)). “Money transmission” expressly reaches virtual currency (control of virtual currency, virtual-currency kiosks, digital wallets, and exchange).
states.regulator: West Virginia Division of Financial Institutions
states.detail: West Virginia’s money transmission statute, W. Va. Code § 32A-2 (the Money Transmission Modernization Act), expressly reaches virtual currency. Section 32A-2-1 defines “control of virtual currency,” “digital wallet,” and “exchange” (which includes virtual currency), and the definition of “money transmission” includes “engaging in the business of owning or operating a virtual currency kiosk.” HB 5353 (2026) amended § 32A-2-1 and related sections to modernize licensing and bring virtual-currency activity, including kiosks, within money-transmission licensure. (The tracker’s prior citation to HB 2585 (2019) was incorrect; HB 2585 was a 2017 money-laundering measure.) The Division of Financial Institutions administers the Act.
states.effective: Money-transmission definition amended to reach virtual currency by HB 2585 (2019); licensing administered by the Division of Financial Institutions
states.sourceText: W. Va. Code § 32A-2-1 defines “control of virtual currency” and includes “engaging in the business of owning or operating a virtual currency kiosk” within money transmission (Money Transmission Modernization Act, as amended by HB 5353 (2026)).

states.name: Vermont
states.framework: Vermont money transmission law (8 V.S.A. ch. 79), amended by Act 110 (2023 Adj. Sess., effective July 1, 2024) to include virtual-currency business activity; virtual-currency kiosk operators are governed by 8 V.S.A. § 2577.
states.detail: Vermont overhauled its money-transmission law through Act 110 (2023 Adj. Sess.), effective July 1, 2024, adopting the Money Transmission Modernization Act and bringing virtual-currency business activity within licensing: persons exchanging, storing, or transmitting virtual currency, or receiving virtual currency or control of it for transmission, as a business must be licensed by the Department of Financial Regulation. Virtual-currency kiosk operators are separately regulated under 8 V.S.A. § 2577, which caps single-customer cash transactions (originally $1,000 per day, raised to $2,000 effective July 1, 2025) and bars new virtual-currency kiosks from operating in Vermont before July 1, 2026 unless the kiosk was licensed and operational on or before June 30, 2024. The Department of Financial Regulation administers the law.
states.effective: Money-transmitter law amended 2024 to formally include virtual-currency business activity (incl. kiosks, 8 V.S.A. § 2577)
states.sourceText: Vermont adopted the Money Transmission Modernization Act via Act 110 (2023 Adj. Sess., eff. July 1, 2024), reaching virtual-currency business activity; virtual-currency kiosks governed by 8 V.S.A. § 2577.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.framework: Wisconsin Sellers of Checks law (Wis. Stat. § 217.03); DFI interprets its authority as not extending to virtual-currency transmission
states.detail: The Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions interprets its authority under Wis. Stat. § 217.03 (the Sellers of Checks law) as not extending to the transmission of virtual currency, so a virtual-currency-only business generally does not need a Wisconsin money-transmitter license. A dealer handling both virtual and fiat currency would still likely need a license for the fiat leg. This exclusion rests on regulator interpretation rather than an express statutory carve-out. Payment-stablecoin issuance remains federally governed by the GENIUS Act.
states.effective: DFI interpretation: authority does not extend to virtual-currency transmission (fiat leg still licensed)
states.sourceText: Wis. Stat. § 217.03 (Sellers of Checks); WI Department of Financial Institutions interpretation.
